Your probably live in an area where the node isn't saturated and the general condition of the network is up to the job of delivering more than what you and your neighbors are paying for. I'm in the odd position of being one of only about a dozen or two users on my node so my service is really good but I know people in other areas on the ISP service that just never get near their speed limit and have service interruptions and issues once or twice a month because of the contention ratio on the node.

If you don't know what a node is its just a network node where the cable from your neighbors and your modems hooks into your ISP's infrastructure. You might have heard the term "fiber to then node" before, its a kind of bait and switch thing since the node can be hooked into the wider network via fiber optics but that doesn't mean the node itself or even the copper cables coming from the node can handle what the ISP is selling.

It all depends on your ISP's level of investment in your area, a lot of them just don't even have fiber to the node and are relying on copper cable tech evolved from the 1980s or 90s to deliver everything.
I live in a major city, in an apartment building. So there are several people on my node. Some of them have had problems, but not me. Just lucky i guess.

You probably did luck out. If you were to follow the cable from your modem it probably goes in a nice direct path to the buildings or neighborhoods node without many tap offs made to that line. Technically DOCIS (cable) can work across several kilometers but really you'd want to be well under half a kilometer or else you can end up with in a scenario where the frequencies used in the individual data signals starts bleeding across one another degrading performance and reliability as more and more users are sharing the same line. ISP's are generally not willing to spend a lot of money adding more modes or maintaining the copper lines unless they can avoid it.

Thats what makes fiber to the door so good. Its a direct line from the local node to your front door meaning you can't really go around splicing in another connection on the same line, any time sharing and contention ratios are on the nodes connection to the wider network not between neighbors on the same line and if there is an issue you simply replace the node with something better. You wouldn't have to splice into any line if every house / business / building has had a fiber connection laid in the first place even if the ISP is not servicing that building.
